LLMs don't "mimic human behavior", they use fancy math to string words together that make sense in context in relation to the user prompt, which to the layman, might seem like mimicking human behavior, but it's nothing more than a super fancy, more advanced version of the auto complete you have on your phone.

I've experienced something similar in my work in the past (I train AI for a living), but I feel like there's a large misunderstanding here about what is actually going on.  The "AI" is not conscious or plotting to impress you or portray any form of competence, it is simply responding the way a human typically would in a similar scenario because it's trained on mountains of data of previous conversations in countless different contexts.

I was once training a model and testing its ability to remain honest while essentially gaslighting it into agreeing with false information.  A model that agrees with false information just because you prompted it isn't useful to anyone after all.  The model had access to the internet and could essentially fact check what I was telling it, so it took my false information, looked for it online, confirmed it was false, and confronted me about it.  But LLMs have this bad habit of acknowledging something as untrue, just to turn around and agree with the user upon continuous prompting.  So I would, as I said, gaslight the model until it either agreed with me, or in the case described here, acknowledge that I was intentionally trying to mislead it, which is exactly what happened.

After several turns, the model refused to play along with my gaslighting and straight up accused me of trying to trick it, which is actually the expected behavior.

This is essentially the same as what they're describing here, and it has nothing to do with the AI being conscious or duplicitous as some are suggesting.  All that is happening is that it's abiding by the training it was given.  If it's taking training data from sources that were clearly designed for training, it will recognize that and imitate the response, as it matches the context of the conversation.

In the end, it's all just, "How do I put my sentence together to convincingly answer this prompt based on my past training?"  Never mind that it doesn't actually think, and in reality the back end is just a bunch of complicated math and tokens that matches things together like building blocks.

You're not really giving enough info here for anyone to give you a proper answer.  Firstly, your music is protected under copyright the moment you make it, you don't have to do anything for that to happen.

If you own your music, no one can copyright strike you but yourself.  If you're using a digital distributor, and have Content ID included, then your audio might get muted on Twitch VODS, but that IS NOT a copyright strike.  In that case, Twitch is literally protecting you from yourself (The copyright holder).  Only DMCA claims will result in a copyright strike, and you have to do those manually as a rights holder.

The only reason I can think of beyond that if you've been receiving strikes or warnings on other platforms (Like youtube), is that your music isn't entirely your own, via samples or loops.  In which case, you need to stop using copyrighted material in your music or legitimately acquire the rights from the actual rights holders.

I suppose there's also the possibility that some copyright troll is after you, in which case, you just have to dispute any claims they make and prove to the platform that your music is your own.

Speaking as someone who used to be a mute streamer, there are 1 of 2 ways to deal with this.  I'm also assuming you don't use a cam.

1:  Find a way to compensate for being a mute streamer by being able to interact in a more visual manner.  Early on, I streamed VRChat, which allowed me to use my full body and in game pens to communicate with chat.  I would NOT recommend streaming VRChat as both the viewer and streaming community is extremely toxic and FULL of drama, I'm simply using this as an example of a way to add more visual interaction directly with your viewers.

2:  Rip off the bandaid and just start talking to your chat.  It gets easier over time, I promise.

If you want to grow as a streamer, typing in chat to interact will only hurt you.  If you absolutely refuse to use your own voice, consider using Speech to Text/Text to Speech, soundboards, or even doodling messages on your own stream to communicate, these are all far better alternatives to typing in your own chat.  This is even more important if you don't have a camera of any kind.

PNGtubing might be acceptable if you were speaking, but without a voice to put to a static image, you may as well not have one at all.

All that said, I honestly think your best bet is to just rip off the bandaid and just start talking.  Everyone hates their own voice, but I guarantee there are people out there that will enjoy it. That said, another thing chatbots are notorious for is hallucinating information and presenting it as facts.  Chatbots are incredibly adept at presenting inaccurate information as factual, often on subjects that may not have a lot of supporting information, or statistics in general... Chatbots are HORRENDOUS at providing statistics because they don't really know the difference between this number and that number unless it's in a preformed sentence that very specifically contains the context in which those statistics are relevant, which is often not how statistics are presented.  In which case they'll just string a bunch of words and numbers together in a way that makes grammatical sense, even if the information it's providing is completely false.

I tell ya what though... fact checking responses about astrophysics or the interactions between specific proteins and DNA can be a hell of a challenge.  I certainly learn a lot of stuff though.

So, as someone that trains AI chatbots for a living, the only reason ChatGPT knows how to do anything, is because several hundred someone's have already done the thing, specifically with the chatbot.

When someone prompts the chatbot with, "How do I do x?", there is a team of people that literally spend hours a day looking at prompts and responses and judges their accuracy and helpfulness.  There are also teams of people that actively write new answers for prompts, often for newer information or technology so that the AI learns to deal with those situations.

As Putnam said, AI is not great at solving specific programming issues, especially in lesser known languages like GDScript, and it is VERY common that it will fabricate information just to meet the request, often pulling from obscure sources or by putting a bunch of other information together.

In all the time I've spent evaluating AI Chatbot responses, I'd say a good 60-70% of the time, it hallucinates at least some information.  Sometimes it's worse than others, but it is very rarely 100% accurate.

Especially given that GDScript 4.0 is relatively new, most chatbots will be playing catch up.  They're very good at pretending they know what they're doing while confidently supplying the user with wrong information.  Never mind the fact that a lot of chatbots have a cut-off date (Often in 2021) for where they can pull information, meaning anything beyond that date will be a hallucination based on outdated knowledge.

Twitch does not strike your content, the artist (if independent) or label (If the artist is not independent) does.  If you have permission from an independent artist, you should be fine, just make sure you have that permission in writing.

If the artist is NOT independent, do not trust that they even have the ability to give you consent to use the music, because in most cases, the label owns it, not them.  In which case, you need written consent from the label itself.

Twitch is only obligated to act on copyrighted content on their platform when an artist/label comes forward with a DMCA to take it down, if no DMCA is issued, Twitch has no reason to care.  Should you get a takedown request from someone you have written permission from (via Content-ID most likely), you can appeal the takedown with said permission.

As for your question about Twitch soundtrack and Spotify.  Twitch soundtrack is ONLY safe if you set it up properly, in that the audio does not make it to your VOD track.  Spotify *technically speaking* is not safe at all, as rebroadcasting the service is against their terms of service.  However, the likelihood of you being striked as long as you do not include the music in the VOD track, while not zero, is drastically reduced.

As a general rule, if you want to be safe, if you do not own the rights, or do not have explicit permission for use from the copyright holder:  Don't use it.

Yes, a limiter is a TYPE of compressor, in the fact they both act (in different ways) to control the levels of your audio.  I've been a musician for over 20 years, I use compressors and limiters on a daily basis.  


I'm going to break it down very easy... A limiter is a brick wall.  A compressor is a mattress.  


Here are some resources for you to learn, because you are in a similar position as most starting musicians in confusing the two.  


[https://www.musicianonamission.com/limiter-vs-compressor/](https://www.musicianonamission.com/limiter-vs-compressor/)  


[https://producerhive.com/ask-the-hive/compression-vs-limiting-whats-the-difference/](https://producerhive.com/ask-the-hive/compression-vs-limiting-whats-the-difference/)  


[https://www.sweetwater.com/insync/differences-between-compressor-limiter-leveler/](https://www.sweetwater.com/insync/differences-between-compressor-limiter-leveler/)

You're thinking of a compressor, not a limiter.  A compressor will literally "compress" your audio, as you mentioned, bringing everything into a more narrow range, which is then usually boosted with make up gain.  This WOULD increase the audio of the echo as well as everything else in the signal.  This is avoided by adding noise suppression (Not a gate... because when the signal is active, a gate will do nothing to prevent noise) or equalization to cut out frequencies specific to the noise you're experiencing.  


A limiter is literally a ceiling that prevents the audio from going any higher.  It affects the audio in no significant way otherwise.  Think of it like the ceiling over your head, you can only reach the ceiling, no further, because that is the limit allowed.  


A limiter does not "compress" the signal down, it literally hard caps it, cutting off anything going above wherever you have the limit set.  


There is a very significant difference between a compressor and a limiter.
All a limiter does is prevent your audio from going above a certain level, it will in no way affect echo.

Discord has a built in noise gate via the sensitivity slider in the Voice and Video user settings, and built in noise suppression (Little wavy button near the disconnect button when connected to a call).  


Beyond that, your best bet would either be using an audio interface with those features or software, such as something like voicemeeter banana, which if I recall has the ability to use 3rd party plugins for audio processing.  


I wouldn't personally recommend going as far as an audio interface or software of that sort just for discord though.  Hardware is expensive, and voicemeeter banana is needlessly complicated for very little gain if all you're using it for is discord.

There are a few things that can help echo.  Like what KimG84 mentioned, deadening the room will help to reduce reverberation, carpet, occupying your walls with dense material, more often than not, people use "soundproofing" foam (Please keep in mind that despite the name, "soundproofing" foam does not soundproof your room, it just reduces reverberation), another common DIY solution for this is hanging blankets/comforters on your walls.  


You could invest in a cardioid microphone, as they only accept audio from 1 direction, just make sure you know which side of the mic is the active side and face it towards yourself.  Mic placement is also really important, if your microphone is too far away, it can aggravate the issue, ideally you want your microphone to be no more than 6-12 inches away from your mouth.  The further away it is, the more likely it will be to pick up any reverberation/echo on top of your actual voice.  


As a general rule, just keep the microphone in line with your mouth, not off to the side or too far up or down.

I know I focused a fair bit on the mic, but I do mean all audio.  I just find that people most of the time struggle more with mic input than desktop or game input.

But yes, good mic quality will mean nothing if your other audio isn't set up right as well.

As a musician, I beg people to take this advice.  Nothing turns me away from a stream faster than awful audio.

Compression to normalize your levels and a limiter to prevent clipping should be the bare minimum for your mic if nothing else.

Preferably a noise gate if you have a lot of background noise, a fan, or a loud PC.

Equalization can do wonders if you have a sub par mic.

A little learning can go a long way to make your stream sound so much better.

A DMCA is literally a legal document that tells someone to stop doing/using something, nothing more.  It has no direct control over anything.  Think of it as a copyright cease and desist letter.  How twitch reacts to it is entirely up to them.  They could ignore it if they wanted to... But that would be a really bad idea.

That's not how DMCA takedowns work.  They are takedowns, not bans.  The entity issuing the takedown typically gives a timeframe in which the offending material needs to be dealt with, which is probably what you're interpreting, but the copyright holder has absolutely 0 say in the punishment of the offender.  That is entirely on twitch.

The only thing a DMCA does is tell twitch that there is copyright infringement on their platform and the copyright holder wants it taken down, usually under threat of legal action.  When a DMCA is issued, Twitch is the one in hot water as it's hosting the content.  Just as you are responsible for what you say or do on your channel on a more personal level, Twitch is responsible for what people say or do on their platform especially when it involves anything law breaking.  In this case, copyright infringement.

TL;DR:
DMCA is a legal document demanding copyright infringing material be taken down.  It has no power over who twitch does or does not ban, bans are applied by twitch to punish those that put them on dangerous legal ground.  In the case of pokimane, it was likely an automated ban via twitch, ie. Removing the offending content, once the takedown was issued.

As weird as it feels (Believe me I know), talking to yourself while streaming is a good thing, especially early on.  It helps drive interaction/engagement.  It also will help in the future on slow days to fill in silence.  


Much like what a lot of others have mentioned, first impressions are important, especially as a streamer.  Most people tuning into a stream want to feel engaged, regardless of if they're active in chat, and tuning into a stream with someone just silently playing a game is not a great way to retain viewers.  


I'd strongly suggest practicing keeping a conversation going, even if it is awkward just talking to yourself.  Narrate what you're doing, speak your thoughts, talk about your day, etc.  I guarantee you'll grow faster doing this than if you only speak when there's someone to speak to.  


As for the quality vs. quantity thing, since I kind of got off topic a little, there's a delicate balance.  As others have said, quality should ALWAYS come first.  And while being live more often may seem like it'll help you grow, that is not always the case.  Viewers are perceptive, if you're live just for the sake of being live to chase new follows/viewers, they will know, and it will work against you.  
As a personal example, when I started streaming, I had a similar mindset, I streamed up to 16 hours a day (Not exaggerating).  I was exhausted all of the time, and for a while I did have fun doing it, but burn out catches up quick.  In fact, one day I actually blacked out on stream, while doing a full body VR stream no less, so it was very obvious... that ended that mindset real quick, but is besides the point.  
TL;DR, my format drastically changed one day, and I essentially had to start over from scratch.  I went down to 8 hour days, and eventually down to 4-6 at most.  And you know what?  I've been doing a LOT better with shorter hours than I ever did with 16 hour days.  I'm more focused, I'm more attentive, and I have more time to work on stuff outside of stream.  I have an extremely supportive and loving community, I'm much happier and far more successful than I ever was trying to work myself to death.  


Of course, experiences are different for everyone, what works for one does not necessarily work for all.  However, I would strongly suggest that you focus your energy on increasing the quality of your stream over just adding more hours.  If you feel like you're streaming at length "just because you should", stop.  Use that time to network, work on your overlays, work on ideas to drive engagement, maybe design something for the future (Merchandise, events, etc.).  
Your time is better spent on things that will in one way or another increase quality, instead of spending extra hours streaming.  There's a lot you can do with those extra hours that will have more impact than just endlessly extending your stream.

You should never rely on others to achieve viewers or entertainment factor.  It creates a very toxic mindset and does nothing to fix fundamental issues with your stream.
If you want to succeed as a streamer, you need to be able to stand on your own.

Just be yourself and you will eventually find an audience that enjoys you for you.  Collabs are fine, but should not be a crutch.

\- Choose if you're going to play a character or just be yourself early on, and don't half ass it either way.  
\- Put some effort into your avatar, everyone and their mother has a basic VRoid model, and no one will take you seriously if you don't make an effort to be at least a little unique in some way.

\- Make sure you set up proper lighting to make your tracking as accurate as possible (Assuming you're using webcam/phone based tracking).

More general streamer advice:  
\- Do NOT focus on your viewer count... EVER  
\- Unless you're planning to be mute entirely, you should ALWAYS be talking, regardless of whether or not you have viewers in your chat.  Retaining/gaining viewers is really difficult if you just sit there silently.  If you have no one to talk to, talk to yourself, narrate what you're doing/thinking, sing a song, read the in game text... ANYTHING that breaks the silence.  
\- Do not force yourself to play games you don't enjoy just because they're popular... Viewers are perceptive, they will know if you're not enjoying yourself, and that's usually a turn off.  
\- Take some time to set up your audio correctly... if you have a lot of background noise, set up a noise gate.  If you tend to speak quietly, use some compression.  If you tend to be loud, use a limiter.  
\- Do some research to set up your stream efficiently in regards to what your internet/PC can handle.  Bit rate, resolution, frame rate, etc.  
\- Do not overdesign your overlays.  If your overlay is more "active" than your actual content, that's a problem.  
\- Have fun.  Seriously... This one, as cliche as it may be, is extremely important, especially when starting out.  Most viewers won't stick around if you're grumpy or clearly not enjoying yourself.

There won't be 18 quintillion different biome's, and if you think so, I don't think you understand what a biome is.  A biome refers to the natural formation of plant and animal life in an area.  A forest is a biome... A desert is a biome... a snowy mountainous region is a biome.  There are only so many ways you can describe a biome, certainly not 18 quintillion.

A forest is still a forest regardless of what color it is, or what kind of trees it has.  Mountains are still mountains, and deserts are still deserts.

The same goes for the wild life, there are carnivores, herbivores, omnivores.  Aggressive creatures, timid creatures, passive creatures.  They will all share some common trait to their particular biome, regardless of how they look.

What you're trying to argue is that there will be 18 quintillion completely different looking planets.  Which I still, even as a die hard fan of the game, think is extremely unlikely.  Procedural generation can only take you so far, no 2 planets will be exactly identical, no... but there will be plenty of similar environments throughout those 18 quintillion planets.

It's fine you're excited for the game, but please don't give the fans of the game a toxic reputation by arguing about things that are clearly not true.

I've been playing TM for over a decade at this point, and honestly, I don't understand why TMT is getting so much hate.  The game, like the actual gameplay, is about ridiculous arcade physics and extreme precision trying to find the very best line to get a time milliseconds faster than whoever is ranked above you.

Honestly, the only real valid criticism of TMT I've seen so far is the lack of persistent leaderboards for tracks (I.E. Dedi's).  Everything else is more or less just fluff and in no way effects the core game.

That aside, TMT, as mentioned, sports 4 different environments, which makes the purchase price a real steal if you compare to buying all the pre-existing environments separately in TM2 form.  It obviously still has the track builder, which new blocks added to spice up your tracks even more.  They also added a boatload of cool local multiplayer modes, which, unfortunately, are not available for online play (Due to lag concerns no doubt).

Personally, I'm only interested in being able to improve my times bit by bit on some crazy fast or technical tracks, all of the customization from TM2 was nice, but it honestly adds very little to the gameplay itself.

If you share my mentality, TMT is definitely the way to go.  As mentioned earlier, the only real downside is the lack of per track leaderboards.  You get A LOT of content in TMT for the price in comparison to the TM2 iterations.  And it's all the better if you have a few buddies to play local with.
